questions.stem: A leaf is a node that:
questions.explanation: No children. (a) is the root; a node with one child (c) is internal.

questions.stem: With height counted in edges, the height of a tree with exactly one node is:
questions.explanation: Height counts edges, and a single node has none. -1 (a) is the empty tree, which makes 1 + max(-1, -1) = 0 work for a leaf.

questions.stem: The largest number of nodes a binary tree of height 3 can hold is:
questions.explanation: Levels 0 to 3 hold at most 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 = 2h+1 - 1. 7 (a) is height 2; 8 (b) is the size of level 3 alone.

questions.stem: The smallest possible height of a binary tree with 100 nodes is:
questions.explanation: ⌊ log2 100 ⌋ = 6: height 6 holds up to 127 nodes, height 5 only 63. 99 (d) is the tallest possible height, a chain.

questions.stem: A binary tree is a binary search tree when, for every node x:
options: x's left child is smaller than x and its right child is larger
every value in x's left subtree is smaller than x, and every value in its right subtree is larger
x is smaller than both of its children
the values read level by level are sorted
questions.explanation: The property is about whole subtrees. (a) is the weaker parent–child check, which W11-M20 shows is not enough; (c) is the heap property of Week 12.

questions.stem: In the tree Q, the right child of the root's left child is:
questions.explanation: The root is 30, its left child 15; 20 > 15 went right. 17 and 25 are 20's children; 8 is 15's left child.

questions.stem: contains(25) on Q compares 25 with how many nodes?
questions.explanation: 30 (go left), 15 (go right), 20 (go right), 25 (found).

questions.stem: The worst-case cost of contains on a BST of n nodes, built by dsa/tree.py from values in an unknown order, is:
questions.explanation: The cost is O(h), and nothing in dsa/tree.py keeps h small: sorted input makes h = n - 1. O(log n) (b) is true only while the tree stays short — on average for random input, or always for a balanced tree.

questions.stem: Which insertion order of 1 to 7 builds the tallest BST?
questions.explanation: 7 first, then 1, then each value between the last two: every node gets one child, a zigzag chain of height 6. (a) and (b) build the perfect tree of height 2 (W11-S2); (c) has height 3.

questions.stem: The pre-order walk of Q is:
questions.explanation: Node, then the whole left subtree, then the right. (a) is in-order, (c) level-order, (d) post-order.

questions.stem: The post-order walk of Q is:
questions.explanation: Both subtrees before the node, so the root 30 is last. (c) is not any of the walks; (d) visits 8 after 17 and 25, which are in a different subtree.

questions.stem: Which walk of any BST lists its values in increasing order?
questions.explanation: Left subtree (all smaller), node, right subtree (all larger): sorted, for every BST.

questions.stem: You save a BST to a file as a list of values, and later rebuild it by inserting the list into an empty tree. To get back the same shape, the list should be the tree's:
questions.explanation: Pre-order lists every node before its descendants, so re-inserting it sends each value down the same path to the same place. The in-order walk (a) is sorted and rebuilds a chain; post-order (c) inserts leaves first, so the first value inserted — a leaf — becomes the root.

questions.stem: Which walk frees a tree safely in a language where you release memory yourself, and evaluates an expression tree?
questions.explanation: Post-order finishes a node's children before the node: free the children while you still hold the links to them, and apply an operator only after both operands have values.

questions.stem: level_order uses a queue rather than the call stack because:
options: a queue uses less memory than recursion
it must visit nodes in order of distance from the root, and the call stack always goes deeper into the most recent node first
recursion cannot visit every node of a tree
the tree stores its nodes in a queue
questions.explanation: Recursion is last in, first out: it finishes the most recent node's subtree before returning. Level-order needs first in, first out — the nodes in the order they were discovered. Memory (a) is not the reason; the queue can be larger than the stack (W11-K3).

questions.stem: During level_order on Q, the largest number of nodes waiting in the queue at one time is:
questions.explanation: After dequeuing 45, and again after dequeuing 20, four nodes wait: 8, 20, 40, 60 and then 40, 60, 17, 25 (W11-S3).

questions.stem: Deleting a node with two children, dsa/tree.py replaces its value with:
options: the largest value in its right subtree
the value of its right child
the smallest value in its right subtree
questions.explanation: The in-order successor. The largest value of the right subtree (a) is too large: everything else in that subtree is smaller than it, yet would sit on its right.

questions.stem: delete(30) on Q. Which value ends up at the root?
questions.explanation: Right once to 45, then left to 40, which has no left child: 40 is the successor and goes to the root. 25 (b) is the predecessor — also a correct choice in general, but not dsa/tree.py's.

questions.stem: The in-order successor of a node with two children never has a left child. Why does that matter to delete?
options: it makes the successor the largest value in the tree
removing the successor is then always a leaf or one-child case, never a second two-children case
it means the successor is always a leaf
questions.explanation: With no left child, the successor is a leaf or has one (right) child, so it is removed by the easy rule. It need not be a leaf (c): in Lecture 11's second example the successor 10 has a right child, 14.

questions.stem: A student's is_valid checks, at every node, only that the left child is smaller and the right child larger. It:
options: accepts some trees that are not BSTs
questions.explanation: It accepts the lecture's tree 8 → 3 → 9, where 9 is a right child of 3 but sits in 8's left subtree. It never rejects a valid BST, and it is O(n) — but wrong.

questions.stem: The expression tree for (2 + 3) * 4 is walked in post-order. The result is:
questions.explanation: Left operand, right operand, operator: 2 3 + 4 *, the postfix form of Lecture 06. (a) is pre-order; (b) is in-order, which has lost the brackets and means 14, not 20.

questions.stem: AVL trees and red-black trees:
options: are the BSTs of dsa/tree.py, under other names
store their nodes in an array, like a heap
are faster than hash tables for every operation
re-shape themselves on insert and delete so that the height stays O(log n)
questions.explanation: Both keep extra data in each node — a height or a colour — and rotate nodes after changes so that the height stays O(log n). They are beyond the bylaw (named, not examined); dsa/tree.py is unbalanced (a).
